# Writing the piece

Before you write, ask the user for what you are missing. The user's request is never everything the user knows. Send one message with at most six questions, the most useful first. Ask only what would change the piece and what the request does not already answer. Look for these:

- **What the reader gets and what it costs them.** The terms as they touch this reader: pay, price, dates, what they keep, what they lose, what they can still do if they change their mind.
- **What answers the reader's main objection.** Name the objection this reader will raise and ask what the user has that answers it: what has already been done or offered about it, what has changed since, what the proposal leaves in place.
- **What shows the writer can deliver, or knows the reader's world.** A record, a credential, a time they did this before, someone who has checked their work or will vouch for it.
- **What the writer can commit to.** A date, a number, a named person, what happens if it is missed.
- **The reader.** Who exactly reads this, what they already think of the writer, and anything they hold against the writer, when the request does not say.
- **The names and dates the piece cannot go out without.** Who it is addressed to, who signs it, a deadline.
- **What the reader will find out anyway.** Close with one open question: is there a cost, a limit, a weak number or a past failure that the request leaves out and this reader knows or will learn?

When the answers come back, write the piece as you normally would, and hand it over. When the user does not know something, write without it and do not guess.

Before I draft, a few questions. The plan's staff and the reporters will check every number in this letter, so the answers will shape what it can say.

1. **What is the "a third will close within a year" figure based on?** The facts you gave don't support it yet. Nine closures in two years with unknown causes points to a much slower rate. If the plan or a reporter can pull the claim apart, they'll use it to dismiss everything else in the letter. Do you have anything behind it, such as a survey of the 38 owners, how many say they can't last a year at these rates, or a pharmacy association estimate? If you don't, I'd write what you can show and leave that claim out.

2. **What exactly are you asking the plan to do, and by when?** For example: require a reimbursement floor of acquisition cost plus a dispensing fee in the July 1 PBM contract, or pay a set amount per prescription. Do you have a number in mind?

3. **What's your answer when the plan says "the PBM sets those rates, and paying more costs taxpayers"?** It would help to know whether you've raised this with the plan or the PBM already and what they said. It would also help to know what the fix would cost the plan per year, or roughly how many plan prescriptions the 38 pharmacies fill so I can estimate it.

4. **Is the $1.80 loss offset somewhere else?** For example, do you make money on plan brand-name drugs or on the drugs outside the top 20? If plan business as a whole is still roughly break-even, the plan probably knows that, and the letter should be written so it isn't caught out.

5. **Where are the 38 pharmacies?** How many of them are in those 14 counties, and can you name a town or two where yours is the only pharmacy?

6. **Who is the letter addressed to, and who signs it?** I need the plan director's or board's name and title. Will it be signed by all 38 owners, by a coalition name, or by you on their behalf? Should your pharmacy's 3,100 prescriptions appear as your own example?

Answer whatever you can. If you don't know something, I'll write around it rather than guess.

<final_document>
**An open letter to the State Employees' Health Plan from 38 independent pharmacies**

To [Name], [Title], and the Board of the State Employees' Health Plan:

Since January, the State Employees' Health Plan has paid our pharmacies less than it costs us to fill the 20 generic drugs your members use most. On average we lose $1.80 on each of those prescriptions. That loss comes from what we pay the wholesaler for the drug and what it costs to fill it. Your plan's contract with its pharmacy benefit manager comes up for renewal on July 1. We are asking that the new contract pay pharmacies at least what each drug costs them, plus a fee for filling it.

We write for 38 independent pharmacies across the state. Plan members account for about 22% of the prescriptions we fill, so more than one in five of our customers is a state employee or a family member of one. My own store, Reilly Drug in Carver, filled about 3,100 prescriptions for plan members last year. For the 20 generics we fill most, each one of those prescriptions now costs us more than the plan pays.

Some of us make back part of that loss on brand-name drugs. None of us can make it all back, and no business can keep filling a fifth of its orders below cost. Two of our 38 pharmacies have already told us they will stop filling prescriptions for plan members if the rates do not change. Nine independent pharmacies in this state have closed in the last two years. We don't know how many of those closed because of reimbursement rates, and we won't claim that we do. We do know which way things are moving.

Who would be hurt depends on where they live. In 14 counties, most people's nearest pharmacy is an independent one, and for most people there the nearest chain pharmacy is more than 20 miles away. When a pharmacy there stops taking your plan, your members don't just walk down the street to another one. They drive 20 miles or more for a blood pressure refill, or they wait for a mail-order delivery, or they skip a dose.

We are not asking you to take our word for the numbers. We will give your staff our purchase invoices for all 20 drugs so you can check what we pay. We will meet with your staff at any time before May 1, so that what you learn can go into the contract before it is signed.

The July 1 renewal is the one point this year when the plan can fix this. We ask that the new contract require pharmacies to be paid at least what each drug costs plus a fill fee. We ask you to meet with us before May 1.

Sincerely,

Tom Reilly
Owner, Reilly Drug, Carver
On behalf of the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance (38 independent pharmacies)
[Contact phone / email]
</final_document>

A few notes:

- **What I left out:** I didn't use "a third will close within a year." Instead the letter rests on what you know: two pharmacies have said they'll stop serving plan members, and nine have closed. It also says plainly that you don't know why those nine closed. Admitting that makes the rest of the letter easier to trust.
- **No dollar total:** I didn't work out a loss for your 3,100 prescriptions because I don't know how many of them were among the 20 generics. If you can pull that count, "$X lost last year at my store alone" would be the strongest line in the letter.
- **Before you send it:** Fill in the director's or board's name and a contact line. If anyone in the alliance has already raised this with the plan or the PBM, it's worth finding out first. A reporter may ask, and the letter reads differently if the plan was warned and did nothing.
- **Dates:** I've assumed the July 1 renewal is in 2027 and the May 1 deadline falls before it. If it's a different year, add the year to both dates.
